listenings.text: A board paper either gets decided or it gets deferred, and the difference is usually not the substance. It is whether the recommendation can be voted on exactly as it is written. My test is simple. Can the chair read your recommendation aloud, word for word, and call for a vote on it? If the answer is no, the item will be discussed and then held over. Papers that ask for support are the ones that come back. Papers that propose a specific action, in a single sentence, are the ones that get decided. The second thing I would say is about safeguards. People put them at the end, as though they were a weakness to be disclosed. Put them in the recommendation. A board that can see the limit of what it is approving approves faster, not more slowly. And write a date on everything, including the day the authority ends.

The first time somebody sent back a draft of mine with be revised instead of is revised, I assumed it was their mistake. I very nearly corrected it back. In my own language the subjunctive is loud: you hear it in the ending of the verb. In English it hides. Nothing is added, something is taken away. The final s disappears, and the sentence looks like a typing error to anyone who learned English by ear. It took me a long time to trust it. What changed was noticing where it appears. Nobody says it in a corridor. It lives in papers, in minutes, in anything that will be read by people who were not in the room, and that is exactly the writing that decides things. When I started using it, the tone of the replies changed before the content did. The same recommendation, in that register, stopped being received as a request.

reading.rtitle: Board Paper 16/4 -- Regional Underwriting Authority, Large Industrial Risks
paras: This paper is submitted for decision. It proposes that regional underwriting authority for large industrial risks be raised from twenty to thirty-five million, and that the increase be reviewed after four quarters rather than made permanent at this stage. The rationale is set out in section two and the safeguards in section three.

The Directorate recommends the increase on two grounds. Cases between twenty and thirty-five million currently take an average of eleven working days to clear the group referral process, and in four instances during the year the broker had placed the risk elsewhere before the referral returned. The Directorate does not argue that the referral process be abandoned. It argues that the threshold no longer matches the market it was written for.

Three safeguards are proposed, and the Directorate regards the third as a prerequisite rather than a refinement. First, that every case written under the raised authority be reported to the group within five working days. Second, that the increase be subject to approval of the reinsurance treaty currently under negotiation. Third, that the authority lapse automatically at the end of the fourth quarter unless the board ratifies it again. The Directorate has given an undertaking to that effect and asks that it be recorded in the minutes.

Two matters remain at the board's discretion. The paper stipulates a single regional limit; the board may prefer that each market be treated separately, which the Directorate would not oppose although it would slow implementation. The paper also proposes that the decision be binding from January. Were the board to prefer a later start, the Directorate requests that the deferral be recorded with a date, since the treaty negotiation will not wait.
reading.source: Board paper -- Commercial Directorate, submitted for the November meeting
